title: Pakistan’s Iran-US balancing Act: Leverage Without Alignment
author: Saima Afzal
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/Pakistan_Flag_at_Mazar-e-Quaid-680x510.jpg)

Photograph Source: Kskhh - Public Domain

Pakistan’s role in the Iran-US conflict is often described as mediation. But
that description misses the more interesting story. Islamabad’s diplomatic
relevance is emerging from a constraint that has shaped its foreign policy for
decades: Pakistan cannot afford to choose cleanly between Iran, the Gulf Arab
states and the United States.

Iran is a neighbour whose stability directly affects Pakistan’s western
border. Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states are critical economic and security
partners. Washington remains an important political and strategic
interlocutor. Pakistan needs functioning relationships with all of them, even
when their interests collide.

What normally looks like a foreign-policy vulnerability has therefore become a
source of leverage. As communication between adversaries becomes more
difficult, Pakistan’s ability to remain connected to competing camps becomes
more valuable.

But this leverage comes with a contradiction. The same relationships that make
Pakistan useful as an intermediary also constrain how far it can go. Islamabad
can facilitate communication, but it cannot easily align with one side without
weakening its credibility with another.

**Balancing is driven by necessity**

Pakistan’s geography places hard limits on its freedom of regional alignment.

It shares a [909-kilometre border](https://www.mofa.gov.pk/tehran-pakistan-
iran-relations) with Iran. Serious instability there could quickly become a
Pakistani security problem through weakened border controls, militant
movement, smuggling or population pressures. At a time when Pakistan already
faces insecurity along its frontier with Afghanistan, another unstable western
border would carry significant costs.

The Gulf matters differently. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and other
Gulf Cooperation Council countries account for more than half of [Pakistan’s
workers’ remittances](https://www.sbp.org.pk/m_policy/2026/MPIC_Apr-2026.pdf).
Millions of Pakistanis live and work across [the
region](https://mofa.gov.pk/middle-east). Gulf states are also important
sources of energy, investment and financial support.

Then there is Washington. The United States no longer occupies the dominant
position in Pakistan’s external relationships that it did during earlier
periods of close strategic cooperation, but it remains too important for
Islamabad to treat as irrelevant.

Pakistan is therefore balancing because the alternatives are costly.

**Economic exposure shapes diplomacy**

The economic dimension of this balancing is easily overlooked.

A prolonged regional conflict would expose Pakistan to higher energy prices,
disrupted trade and more expensive shipping. The [Strait of
Hormuz](https://www.eia.gov/international/analysis/special-
topics/World_Oil_Transit_Chokepoints) remains one of the world’s most
important energy chokepoints, while insecurity around Bab al-Mandab can affect
shipping between Asia, the Middle East and Europe.

For an energy-importing economy with limited room to absorb external shocks,
these disruptions are not abstract geopolitical risks. They can feed directly
into inflation, foreign-exchange pressures and domestic economic instability.

Pakistan’s preference for de-escalation is therefore closely aligned with its
own economic and security interests. Islamabad has substantial material
reasons to prevent a wider war.

It needs Iran to remain stable without alienating the Gulf. It needs Gulf
security without becoming part of an explicitly anti-Iranian alignment. And it
needs a functional relationship with Washington without allowing that
relationship to determine its regional policy.

That is not neutrality. It is strategic balancing under pressure.

**Access is not the same as influence**

The Iran-US confrontation has demonstrated the value of this position.

Pakistan can communicate with Tehran while remaining engaged with Washington
and Gulf capitals. When direct diplomacy becomes politically difficult, that
access can provide channels for proposals, messages and possible compromises.

The June 2026 Islamabad [Memorandum of
Understanding](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/white-house-sends-
text-interim-us-iran-agreement-us-congress-2026-06-18/) demonstrated both the
possibilities and the limits of this role. Pakistan helped create negotiating
space and a framework for continued diplomacy. But it could not guarantee
implementation once Washington and Tehran returned to confrontation.

The distinction between access and influence matters.

Pakistan may be able to bring messages across political divides, but it cannot
determine how Washington calculates the costs of military pressure or how
Tehran evaluates deterrence, sanctions and its nuclear programme. Mediation
does not erase the underlying distribution of power.

[Pakistan’s diplomatic](https://mofa.gov.pk/press-releases/transcript-of-the-
press-briefing-by-the-spokesperson-on-thursday-16th-july-2026) value is
therefore significant, but its influence ultimately depends on decisions made
in Washington, Tehran and other regional capitals. Its strength lies in
preserving channels through which those decisions can be communicated, tested
and potentially reconciled.

**The risk of strategic overextension**

The more difficult question is whether Pakistan can preserve the autonomy that
makes its mediation possible.

Closer defence cooperation with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf partners
strengthens Pakistan’s regional position. Yet if Tehran begins to view
Islamabad primarily through the lens of Gulf security competition, Pakistan’s
credibility as an intermediary could weaken.

Moving too far in the other direction would create its own problems. Excessive
accommodation of Iranian concerns could unsettle Gulf partners whose economic
and security relationships remain critical to Pakistan.

Washington presents a similar dilemma. American confidence in Islamabad can
increase Pakistan’s diplomatic usefulness, but preserving visible policy
independence remains important to its credibility with other regional actors.

Pakistan therefore gains influence by resisting exclusive alignment.

This does not require equidistance between Iran, the Gulf and the United
States. Such equidistance would be unrealistic. It requires enough strategic
autonomy for each side to believe that maintaining a relationship with
Islamabad remains worthwhile.

**Leverage without alignment**

Pakistan’s experience points to a broader reality of an increasingly
fragmented international order. States do not always gain influence by
choosing a bloc. Some gain it by maintaining relationships across competing
blocs.

But there are limits to this strategy.

Strategic connectivity produces influence only when competing actors continue
to trust the intermediary’s access. Once balancing is perceived as alignment,
the diplomatic value of that connectivity begins to disappear.

Pakistan cannot determine whether Washington and Tehran ultimately choose
compromise or confrontation. Nor can it insulate itself completely from the
consequences of their decisions. What it can do is preserve communication
across political divides and resist pressure to reduce a complicated regional
environment to a choice between rival camps.

For Islamabad, this strategy combines diplomatic choice with the realities of
geography and economic interdependence. Iran will remain its neighbour. The
Gulf will remain central to its economic interests. Washington will continue
to matter. None of these relationships can easily substitute for the others.

That is why Pakistan’s mediation should be understood neither as simple
neutrality nor as an abstract pursuit of peace. It is diplomacy grounded in
national interest and sustained by strategic connectivity.

The irony is that necessity can produce leverage. Pakistan’s need to remain
connected to competing powers gives it influence when those powers can no
longer communicate easily with one another.

But that leverage will survive only as long as Islamabad can maintain the
distinction between balancing relationships and choosing sides.
